content: 1. General Danger Signs: A child presenting with an inability to breastfeed or drink, lethargy, reduced consciousness, or convulsions should be considered critically ill and requires immediate medical attention. 2. Severe Pneumonia: Hospital admission is necessary. Administer oxygen if oxygen saturation is below 90%. Provide the recommended antibiotic therapy. Treat high fever if present. 3. Fast Breathing Criteria: For children aged 2–11 months: ≥50 breaths per minute. For children aged 1–5 years: ≥40 breaths per minute. 4. Chest Indrawing: This is a significant sign of respiratory distress and should be evaluated promptly. 5. Management of Pneumonia: For non-severe cases, home care is appropriate with oral antibiotics. Educate caregivers on when to seek immediate medical attention for worsening symptoms. Follow up after three days to assess improvement. 6. Cough or Cold Without Pneumonia: Provide supportive care, such as safe remedies to soothe the throat and relieve cough. Advise caregivers to return if symptoms worsen or persist beyond 14 days. Avoid unnecessary medications like antibiotics, atropine, codeine derivatives, or alcohol-based remedies. 7. Investigations for Pneumonia: Obtain a chest X-ray if possible to identify complications like pleural effusion, empyema, or pneumothorax. 8. Oxygen Therapy: Administer oxygen to children with oxygen saturation below 90%. Use nasal prongs as the preferred delivery method for infants. Monitor oxygen therapy with pulse oximetry and discontinue when saturation stabilizes above 90%. 9. Antibiotic Therapy: For severe pneumonia, administer intravenous ampicillin (or benzylpenicillin) and gentamicin for at least five days. Adjust treatment based on clinical response and diagnostic findings. 10. Supportive Care: Clear nasal or throat secretions gently if they obstruct breathing. Encourage breastfeeding and oral fluids. Use nasogastric feeding if the child cannot drink adequately. Avoid overhydration to prevent complications. 11. Monitoring: Hospitalized children should be assessed by a nurse every three hours and by a doctor at least twice daily. Improvement should be evident within two days, including slower breathing, reduced fever, and better feeding. 12. Complications of Pneumonia: Common complications include pleural effusion, empyema, and lung abscess. Pleural effusions should be drained unless very small, and fluid analysis should guide further management. 13. Persistent Symptoms: If fever and other symptoms persist despite treatment, consider testing for HIV or tuberculosis, especially in malnourished children. 14. Bronchiolitis: This viral lower respiratory infection is most severe in young infants and may require oxygen therapy and supportive care. Episodes of wheezing may persist for months but usually resolve. 15. Asthma: Characterized by recurrent wheezing and reversible airway obstruction. Treat with bronchodilators and anti-inflammatory drugs. Antibiotics are only indicated if pneumonia is present. 16. Wheezing: Wheezing in young children is often due to viral infections. Assess for pneumonia if fever or chest indrawing is present. Rapid-acting bronchodilators can help determine the underlying cause and guide treatment. 17. Discharge Criteria: Children with severe pneumonia can be discharged when respiratory distress resolves, oxygen saturation is stable above 90%, and they are feeding well. 18. Infection Control: Handwashing and isolation during hospital stays can reduce cross-infection risks, especially during epidemics. 19. Follow-Up: Arrange follow-up visits to monitor recovery and address risk factors like malnutrition, indoor air pollution, and parental smoking. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the diagnosis, management, and follow-up of respiratory illnesses in children, emphasizing evidence-based practices and patient safety.
